title: The Astronomer Who Invented Global Navigation
event_summary: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi completed the Zij-i Ilkhani (Ilkhanic Tables) at the Maragheh Observatory, the most advanced astronomical facility in the world, funded by Mongol ruler Hulagu Khan. Al-Tusi's mathematical innovation—the 'Tusi couple,' which converted circular motion into linear motion—solved a fundamental problem in planetary modeling that had defeated astronomers for a thousand years. The observatory brought together scholars from China, Byzantium, and the Islamic world in history's first truly international scientific collaboration, producing star catalogs and planetary tables of unprecedented accuracy.
why_forgotten: The Mongol Empire's eventual fragmentation scattered institutional memory, and European Renaissance astronomers like Copernicus adopted al-Tusi's mathematical techniques without clear attribution. Colonial-era historiography credited the heliocentric revolution entirely to European genius, burying the direct transmission chain from Maragheh through Byzantine intermediaries to Cracow. The observatory itself fell into ruin within decades of al-Tusi's death, leaving no visible monument to anchor public memory.
why_it_matters: The Tusi couple appears almost identically in Copernicus's De Revolutionibus, meaning the mathematical engine of the Copernican Revolution has Maragheh DNA—reshaping our understanding of how modern science actually emerged through cross-civilizational exchange rather than isolated European brilliance. The Ilkhanic Tables were used by navigators across Asia for centuries, directly enabling the maritime trade networks that preceded and shaped the Age of Exploration. Maragheh's model of state-funded, multinational scientific collaboration prefigured institutions like CERN by seven hundred years.
